title: A suitable common interface
source_text:
\subsection{A suitable common interface}

Define a small straight-line block whose operand references either a boundary
port or an earlier local node. Its 14 boundary ports include the constants one
and two; its semantic specification is the common free-carrier finalizer.
Then establish four facts:

\begin{enumerate}
\item A block evaluator agrees with insertion into a parent topological DAG
when the boundary values agree.
\item This one 99-node block evaluates to the common \code{ratioValue}.
\item Each existing parent suffix is the exact reference-instantiation of
the block.
\item The existing front-end register lemmas supply the boundary values.
\end{enumerate}

Insertion should instantiate references directly, adding no copy gates.
Retain equality with each pinned parent node list, the operation counts, and
the output index. Source-level sharing must not change the measured equation
or hide a changed literal coefficient tuple.

The typing issue is real: Split has 12 fixed inputs and Gap has 11, while the
existing \code{NodeRel} is formulated for equal input and fixed-input arities.
Since the common tail does not read fixed-input leaves, a boundary-port block
captures the exact shared object without coercing the two parent node types.

Put the common block below both specializations in the import graph. It should
depend on generic DAG semantics and common finalizer algebra, not on either
entire specialized circuit. A module cycle would cancel much of the intended
simplification.

This proposal reduces duplicated proof about 99 nodes. It does not remove
99 arithmetic operations from either Diophantine construction, and no such
size improvement is claimed. The new generic machinery must be charged against
any eventual source reduction.

source_text:
\subsection{Do not weaken arbitrary-code soundness}

The existing \code{AnnotatedLineScan.scan_sound} applies to arbitrary natural
codes and arbitrary fuel. A theorem about \code{state rows history} covers
only states arising from the chosen encoding. The latter cannot replace the
former. Keep an invariant on raw numeric states, prove one-step preservation
using the actual local checker, and lift it through the common iteration
theorem. Use encoded-list simulation for completeness and sufficient-fuel
arguments. This separation removes repeated induction without introducing a
parser assumption.

The same distinction applies to finished states. The generic interface does
not assume that a rejecting state and every completed state are distinct.
Any distinction needed by the final acceptance test must remain an explicit
property of the concrete numeric implementation.

title: Share residual-system facts before merging compilers
source_text:
\section{Share residual-system facts before merging compilers}
\label{sec:squares}

Three files contain the same private \code{eval_sumExpressions} induction:
\src{DAGQuartic}{, }
\src{NaturalDAGQuartic}{, and }
\src{QuadraticRegisterSystem}{.}
Publish it in the syntax layer and prove once, for an arbitrary finite
residual family $r_i$, that
\[
 \left(\sum_i r_i^2\right)(v)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \forall i,\ r_i(v)=0
 \qquad\text{over }\mathbb Z.
\]
Each compiler's \code{expression_zero_iff} then only unfolds its residual
family and invokes this interface. The concrete proof is in the proposed
\code{CircuitCoreRefactors.lean}; its checked status is listed separately.

The codomain restriction is substantive. Over a general commutative ring,
a sum of squares need not vanish only when each square does. For example,
$1^2+i^2=0$ over the complex numbers. The internal-omega theorem in
\code{ObjectResidualSquares} uses the object theory's positive/negative
semiring interpretation and order. It cannot be replaced by the integer
lemma without an appropriate proof of transfer.

The signed and nonnegative DAG compilers share gate semantics and degree

natural parts; the single-wire natural compiler requires a nonnegativity
invariant. Common RHS syntax and residual lemmas are good targets. A universal

than silently adding nonnegativity to the signed theorem. Exact witness counts

\section{Use a common DAG invariant theorem selectively}

\src{ArithmeticDAGSemantics}{ already proves the local node equation and
uniqueness of a value table satisfying those equations.}
\src{ArithmeticDAGDegree}{ and }
\src{NaturalDAGQuartic}{ repeat the corresponding topological strong induction
for degree and nonnegativity.}

A general invariant has the following mathematical form. Let $P(i,r)$ be a
property of register $i$ and value $r$. If each gate at $i$ preserves $P$
whenever $P$ holds at all its dependency registers, then $P$ holds at every
register in the actual run. Topology supplies the strict predecessor bound;
\code{run_node_equation} supplies the gate equation.

\begin{Lean}
-- Essential local premise of run_invariant:
∀ i < nodes.length, ∀ values,
  (∀ j ∈ (nodes.getD i (.literal 0)).dependencies,
    P j (values j)) →
  P i ((nodes.getD i (.literal 0)).evalAt p x values)
\end{Lean}

The supplied light \code{DAGInvariant.lean} and larger
\code{CircuitCoreRefactors.lean} show proposed clients for degree bounds,
semantic-table uniqueness, and nonnegative runs. This also supports future
range bounds and symbolic normal-form certificates.

This is not an immediate net line-saving result in the measured examples.
Three original declarations occupy 42 lines and 2,083 bytes; a proposed helper
plus three replacements occupy 45 lines and 2,296 bytes under the supplied
formatting. Longer example names contribute to the latter figure. The benefit
is concentrating the induction invariant and topology bookkeeping. Adopt it
when additional clients justify the common interface, or when it makes a
particularly fragile proof substantially easier to maintain.

\code{value_map}. These are valuable for genuine ring homomorphisms, but

Instead, parameterize the existing simulation proof by its reference map,

The row-identity families in Gap, Split, and Native each compare low-degree
source residuals with coefficient representations. A normalized sparse
quadratic syntax is a bounded, reviewable target for a certificate checker.
Check its equality to the independently supplied source recipe. Avoid expanding
the full high-degree finalizer into a polynomial normal form: that destroys
the sharing which the circuit representation was designed to preserve.

title: Preserve cancellation-aware degree arguments
Represent elementary row operations once
source_text:
\section{Represent elementary row operations once}

\src{SplitCertificate59}{ proves \code{transformed_zero_iff} by explicitly
handling all 22 coordinates in both directions.}
Most coordinates are unchanged; two rows are modified by adding a different
row. The proof is an instance of a very small general fact.

For a row family $r:I\to R$ and distinct indices $d,s$, define
\[
 (\operatorname{addAt}_{d,s}r)(k)=
 \begin{cases}r(d)+r(s)&k=d,\\r(k)&k\ne d.\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
 (\forall k,\ (\operatorname{addAt}_{d,s}r)(k)=0)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\forall k,\ r(k)=0).
\]
The forward direction first reads the unchanged source row $s$, obtaining
$r(s)=0$, and then reads the destination row. No cancellation or inverse
operation is necessary: a type with addition and the usual zero laws suffices.
Distinctness of $d$ and $s$ is essential to this argument.

\code{RowOperations.lean} checks this generic theorem and the corresponding
fact for a surjective reindexing. The intended concrete refactoring expresses
the transformed family as two elementary row additions, then invokes this
theorem twice. The final reordering uses the existing
\code{rowOrder_surjective}. The equality between the actual transformed
syntax and those elementary operations remains to be established; it is the
finite binding certificate, not an assumption to omit.

This is preferable to introducing a full matrix library solely for two row
additions. If later transformations include arbitrary invertible linear
combinations, a matrix-based zero-set preservation theorem becomes appropriate.
The current case supports a much smaller interface.

title: Simplify object-model proof transport without changing strength
An especially small arity-polymorphism improvement

source_text:
\subsection{Build on the algebraic interfaces already present}

The project already has \code{ObjectOmegaSemiring},
\code{ObjectNaturalOrder}, \code{GatesSemiring}, and \code{QuarticSemiring}.
The next step is to share model-independent finite-index and renaming facts
between their callers. For example, conjunction of row families has the same
index argument in \code{ObjectQuadraticSystem} and
\code{QuadraticRegisterComposition}.

Two constraints affect the design. First, directly importing
\code{ObjectNaturalOrderedSemiring} into \code{ObjectResidualSquares} would

\section{Improve the current-window API where coherence already exists}

\src{CurrentPolynomialWindow2011}{ already contains a substantial
\code{Facts} structure tying one source assignment, one window length,
one Boolean word, one carry function, and one digit function together.}
That design should be reused. The proposed improvement is to expose smaller
proved views and derived quantities, not to introduce a competing record.

Examples include a named temporal-shift expression, a view containing the
four carry/mask facts needed by a local decoding lemma, and named fields for
the source-coordinate transport. Construct \code{Facts} using named fields
instead of a long positional tuple when this helps future edits. The latter
does not necessarily shorten source, but makes an added field easier to audit.

\src{CurrentDecodedWindow2011}{ correctly derives count and phase from the
same arithmetic facts before invoking the cell decoder.}
Keep that order. A ``simplified'' cell interface that assumes occupation or
phase before the relevant polynomial theorem supplies them would make the
composition circular. In particular, the decoded-cell alternatives still allow
empty cells; the new interface must not quietly assume that every cell selects
a tile.

At the arithmetic boundary, derive reusable conversion facts once. Natural
subtraction is truncated, integer subtraction is not, and \code{ZMod} values
are representatives modulo the full window length. An unconditional rewrite
between these interpretations is usually wrong. Good helper statements carry
the exact positivity or range premise that makes the conversion valid.
Then use \code{omega} for the remaining linear natural-number arithmetic and
\code{ring} for equalities after entering the ring domain.

This keeps representation changes separate from mathematical content. It is
also more robust than adding long lists of low-level cast and subtraction
lemmas to every downstream \code{simp} call.

One especially local example is congruence weakening. The result
\code{CurrentClause2011.reflected_weight_mod} works modulo 2048;
\code{CurrentEarlyPadding2011.reflected_mod_sixteen} repeats the same
selector/nonselector analysis modulo 16. The latter should follow through
\code{Nat.ModEq.of_dvd}, since $16\mid2048$. The early-padding module already
imports the clause module. The two local selector functions have the same
defining equations; their definitional identification or a shared definition
must be checked. This is a source-inspected one-line-wrapper opportunity,
not a replayed project edit.

title: Finite checking and generated proof design
source_text:
\section{Finite checking and generated proof design}

The desired trust boundary is ordinary Lean proof checking. A generator may
produce a finite table, a reference map, or a proposed algebraic certificate;
Lean must verify the assertion that table is used to justify. Keep certificate
data independent of the conclusion and preserve the current endpoint axiom
audits.

Several practical experiments are worthwhile:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Split large closed checks into stable pieces.} Compare a single
\code{decide} over a large nested finite predicate with a small indexed family
of checks or a partitioned certificate. This may change resource use, but
neither short source nor many small cases guarantees faster replay.
\item \textbf{Reduce data selection before symbolic branching.} For row
coefficient proofs, choose the finite row and simplify vector indexing before
splitting conditionals. Otherwise a tactic may inspect branches belonging to
unselected rows.
\item \textbf{Keep high-level cuts explicit.} Do not make large register
expansion lemmas global simp rules. Use local lists of established semantic
facts and prove small ring identities at the resulting boundaries.
\item \textbf{Edit the generator with its output.} Check byte-for-byte
regeneration and compile the emitted proof. A passing generator test alone
does not certify its mathematical output.
\item \textbf{Retain compatibility wrappers when useful.} Public theorem
names referenced by checks can remain as thin corollaries of a generic proof.
Private wrappers can be removed after confirming their scope.
\end{enumerate}

These recommendations do not require replacing kernel reduction with
\code{native_decide}. The current source avoids that tactic. A tactic or
certificate generator should emit ordinary checked proof terms if the existing
axiom footprint is to be retained. Changes to trust assumptions should be
explicit design decisions, not incidental source-shortening techniques.

source_text:
\subsection{Expose assignment naturality once}

\src{Representation}{155--231} repeatedly proves function extensionality to show that renaming variables commutes with the assignment combining source variables and witnesses. Conjunction and disjunction each repeat a left and a right version. \src{QuarticCompiler}{95--98} already contains a narrower private \code{assignment_comp} lemma.

Generalize that idea at the earlier representation boundary:
\begin{Lean}
theorem natAssignment_comp_map
    (v : sigma' -> Nat) (w : tau' -> Nat)
    (f : sigma -> sigma') (g : tau -> tau') :
    natAssignment v w ∘ Sum.map f g =
      natAssignment (v ∘ f) (w ∘ g) := by
  funext i
  cases i <;> rfl
\end{Lean}
Pair the lemma with \code{Expr.eval_rename}, and the client proofs can normalize assignments without constructing fresh extensionality proofs. The proposed patch saves 25 lines in the complete module, counting the new helper.

Start with explicit \code{simp only} uses. A new global simplification attribute is unnecessary for realizing this saving, and a deliberate normalization direction is easier to review. The executable expressions, witness counts, and coordinate injections should stay identical. The artifact table records both the generic lemma check and the complete-file patch check separately.

title: The five-residual theorem
source_text:
\subsection{The five-residual theorem}

\src{ShortSystem}{64--91} proves that a sum of five integer residual squares vanishes exactly when all five residuals vanish. Its forward proof derives each squared residual separately with \code{nlinarith}, supplying the same nonnegativity facts repeatedly.

Write the residual vector as
\[
r=(n_0-1,\ n_1-1,\ n_a-1,\ n_s-1,\ n_k n_t-1).
\]
Then use the already available \code{Finset.sum_mul_self_eq_zero_iff} and simplify the five-element sum. The checked \code{ResidualSumChecks.lean} states the same theorem against the original \code{ShortSystem.residualSum}; its body is a single specialization followed by simplification. The exact replacement compiled on Lean 4.32.0. The supplied patch also adds the required finite-sum imports; the full patched module has not been rebuilt.

This improves the proof's explanation: the conclusion follows from the zero criterion for a sum of squares over the integers. It also avoids five solver calls on a repeated nonlinear expression. No build-time improvement is asserted without measurement. The total ordered-ring assumptions are essential to the shared theorem; the statement cannot be transplanted unchanged to arbitrary commutative rings.

title: Share the syntax-level theorem across compilers
source_text:
\subsection{Share the syntax-level theorem across compilers}

There is a second, more reusable opportunity. \src{DAGQuartic}{83--98}, \src{NaturalDAGQuartic}{110--126}, and \src{QuadraticRegisterSystem}{70--87} repeat a private evaluation lemma for \code{QuarticSyntax.sumExpressions}, then specialize the same sum-of-squares argument.

Place a common theorem near \code{QuarticSyntax} for an arbitrary residual family \code{Fin n -> Expr sigma}:
\[
\operatorname{eval}\!\left(\sum_i r_i r_i\right)(v)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall i,\ \operatorname{eval}(r_i)(v)=0.
\]
Each compiler's \code{expression_zero_iff} then becomes one application. The residual definitions continue to show which local equations are being imposed; the helper only centralizes how conjunction is represented by squares. \code{CircuitRefactoring.lean} supplies the common theorem and both signed-DAG and natural-DAG clients.

The same approach applies to cost proofs. \src{DAGQuartic}{166--178} has a general sum-cost bound, while \src{QuarticCost}{65--74} has a special bound of five operations per term. Move the more general bound to a lower layer and derive the specialized result. Avoid a dependency from basic syntax back into a particular compiler.

\src{GapCircuitTranslation66}{16--76} and \src{SplitCircuitTranslation59}{16--76} each exclude one row from the ordinary finite \code{NodeRel} certificate, then handle that row with a custom multiplication rewrite. The exceptional rows are 421 and 452. Their issue is operand order.

title: Share iteration laws without changing the programs
Replace acceptance equivalences by exact numeric values
source_text:
\subsection{Replace acceptance equivalences by exact numeric values}

\code{AnnotatedRenameLocal} and \code{AnnotatedBoundLocal} already establish that their numeric classifier is Boolean and that it equals one precisely when the row validator accepts. Their scanner clients reconstruct the rejecting value repeatedly; see \src{AnnotatedRenameScan}{57--69} and the parallel bound-scanner proof.

Combine the facts once:
\[
(n=0\lor n=1)\ \wedge\ (n=1\leftrightarrow b=\mathrm{true})
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
n=\begin{cases}1&b=\mathrm{true},\\0&b=\mathrm{false}.
\end{cases}
\]
\code{BooleanCore.lean} checks the generic lemma. The scanner proof can then rewrite the numeric result directly before splitting on the Boolean value.

Both premises matter. The equivalence $n=1\leftrightarrow b=\mathrm{true}$ alone says nothing about whether a rejected value is zero or two. Also retain the raw-natural Booleanity theorem: a result only on canonical encoded rows does not replace the raw-code soundness argument.

title: Derive weaker moduli from stronger ones
A half-radix shift needs arithmetic, not sixteen cases
source_text:
\subsection{A half-radix shift needs arithmetic, not sixteen cases}

The half-radix cases of \code{NativeCyclicRotation.shiftDigits} reduce to the exact identity, for $s>0$,
\[
(sa)\bmod(2s)+\left\lfloor\frac{sb}{2s}\right\rfloor
=s(a\bmod2)+\left\lfloor\frac b2\right\rfloor.
\]
From $b\le3$, the result is at most $s+1$, because $a\bmod2\le1$ and $b/2\le1$. If $s$ is even, its parity is exactly $b/2$. This removes the need to enumerate both current and predecessor digits. It even shows that the bound on the current digit is unnecessary for these scalar conclusions.

\code{HalfShiftArithmetic.lean} proves the identity, bound and parity result using only \code{Std.Tactic}; all three compile. The intended clients are \src{NativeCyclicRotation}{100--116} and lines 160--165. Applying them to the cyclic predecessor still requires the original positivity and indexing facts. The checked scalar theorem is not a completed replacement of those project clients.

title: Make the padding witness conditional
source_text:
\subsection{Make the padding witness conditional}

In \code{NativePreliminaryCount2011.total_le_one_all_phases}, the padding function is quantified outside the hypothesis saying that it is relevant only in middle phases. As a consequence, \src{CurrentCount2011}{46--54} constructs an artificial zero function in the other phases.

Change the interface from a globally supplied function with a conditional property to a conditional existence:
\[
7\le\mathrm{phase}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{phase}\le10
\ \longrightarrow\ \exists u,\ \mathrm{PaddingFacts}(u).
\]
Destruct the witness only inside the middle-phase branch. The outer caller can forward its real padding-existence theorem directly. The supplied two-file candidate saves ten physical lines and removes a dummy witness. \code{ConditionalPadding.lean} states an alternative theorem against the existing lower-level count lemmas.

This is an API change, unlike the proof-body-only patches. It needs all callers to be checked. Only one production caller was found at this snapshot. The underlying mathematical requirement is unchanged: the function is only needed when the middle-phase condition holds.

title: Use one exact decomposition interface
source_text:
\subsection{Use one exact decomposition interface}

The repository already has \code{CurrentPolynomialWindow2011.Facts}; a recommendation simply to ``bundle the window facts'' would repeat existing work. A useful refinement is a small normalization view centered on
\[
R=d+B c,\qquad 0\le d<B.
\]
It gives $c=\lfloor R/B\rfloor$, and if $m\mid B$ it gives $d\bmod m=R\bmod m$. If $R<B$, the outgoing carry is zero. \code{NormalizationArithmetic.lean} checks these three scalar facts. They apply to repeated modular rewrites in \src{CurrentClause2011}{160--166}, \src{CurrentEarlyPadding2011}{251--258}, and \src{CurrentPhaseParity2011}{113--117}.

The strict digit bound is needed for the quotient formula. The decomposition equation by itself allows many digit/carry pairs. The modular projection needs the divisibility premise, while the small-total reset can derive the necessary digit bound. This interface must retain the incoming carry as part of $R$ and must not introduce a fictitious zero starting carry into a cyclic stream.

There is also duplicated extraction of canonical digit witnesses in \src{CurrentSparseDigits2011}{118--129} and \src{CurrentHighDigits2011}{141--152}. A shared witness-producing lemma can return the length, digit family and its actual normalization facts once. That is preferable to asking every later argument to destruct the same existential representation independently.

\subsection{A definable-induction transport lemma}

The \code{Object*} modules repeatedly use \code{omega_ind} through an explicit formula and its satisfaction equivalence. Examples are \src{ObjectAdditionLaws}{52--72}, lines 86--105 and 126--150, together with \code{ObjectMultiplicationLaws} and \code{ObjectDistributivity}. Their arithmetic induction steps are substantive; the repeated semantic transport can be shared.

A proposed \code{omega_ind_of_spec} should take an actual formula, environment, and a theorem identifying satisfaction of that formula with the desired predicate. It transports the base and step cases to \code{omega_ind}, then transports the result back. Each arithmetic proof can work with its named semantic relation while displaying the formula that witnesses definability.

This is an architectural proposal. Arbitrary induction on every external predicate over the model's naturals is too strong. Replacing it with induction on Lean's \code{Nat} is also inappropriate when the internal model may be nonstandard. The supplied specification of the defining formula is the essential boundary. \code{ObjectOmegaSemiring} already supplies a semiring interface; adding another semiring abstraction would miss the actual repeated work below it.

Several endpoints repeat the same sequence: apply \code{completeness_inf_context}, obtain the model, build its arithmetic axioms with \code{axioms_of_zfc_model}, and invoke \code{seal_valid} before the local semantic argument. See \src{ObjectAdditionLaws}{183--206}, \src{ObjectDistributivity}{132--156}, and \src{ObjectMultiplication}{198--219}. A model-extraction lemma is itself duplicated privately in \code{ObjectArithmetic} and publicly in \code{ObjectMultiplication}.

Move that extraction theorem earlier and add one semantic-validity-to-sealed-provability bridge. Its hypotheses must quantify over all the models and environments required by the existing completeness theorem, and its conclusion must be the same sealed formula. Callers can then provide just the arithmetic argument.

Keep endpoints with a nonempty context separate unless a context-aware bridge is proved. This refactor should make the exact assumptions easier to see. It does not establish a missing arithmetic/compiler connection or create a new internal consistency result by changing the presentation of the endpoint.

title: Prefer a stable simplification boundary
source_text:
\subsection{Prefer a stable simplification boundary}

The most maintainable short proofs usually unfold one semantic layer and use named facts for the next. Keep executable code, expression evaluation, arithmetic normal forms and model interpretation as separate simplification layers. A proof which unfolds every implementation at once may be shorter in source while producing larger goals and coupling distant modules.

Use \code{simp?} during development to discover a sufficient explicit set; retain \code{simp only} where stable dependencies matter. The Lean manual documents both the explicit set and ordinary simplifier behavior.\footnote{\url{https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/The-Simplifier/Invoking-the-Simplifier/}; accessed 26 October 2026. Exact examples in this packet were checked against Lean 4.32.0.} Do not mechanically replace every \code{simp} with a long explicit list. Small, conventional algebraic normalizations are often clearer with the ordinary simplifier.

Use \code{omega} for bounded natural/integer arithmetic after the mathematical structure is exposed. Use \code{ring} for algebraic identities, \code{nlinarith} where inequalities genuinely need nonlinear combination, and \code{decide +kernel} for closed finite certificates when appropriate. Replacing all proofs by broad automation would obscure the very interfaces this report recommends.
